issues: Both GCHQ quotes --check FOUND. The Williamson page says Cocks and Williamson worked on 'Non-Secret Encryption, following a question by James Ellis', that Cocks devised RSA and Williamson key exchange, and that the academics found it 'at almost the same time'. The Ellis page gives 'The discovery in 1973' and says Ellis died 25 November 1997, 'just a month before the public announcement', which is consistent with December 1997.

Nuance, not an error: Williamson's key exchange dates from about 1974, so 'early 1970s' is at the edge of that description, but GCHQ itself dates the discovery to 1973. Diffie and Hellman's 'New Directions' (November 1976) was the first open publication; Merkle's puzzles paper was submitted in 1975 but published in 1978. The claim holds.

fieldFixes.correction: The Guardian's 13 January 2017 story described a design choice — WhatsApp by default re-encrypts and resends undelivered messages when a contact's key changes, without first asking the sender to verify. Signal's Moxie Marlinspike called the 'backdoor' label false. The Guardian dropped the word within hours, and after a review by its readers' editor, who found the story 'overstated its case', it extensively amended the article on 28 June 2017. The article now describes 'a design feature' and says systematic surveillance is unlikely.

issues: Both quotes --check FOUND. The Sweeney header reads 'Carnegie Mellon University, Data Privacy Working Paper 3. Pittsburgh 2000' and the paper uses 1990 census data. The Golle PDF reads 'WPES'06, October 30, 2006, Alexandria, Virginia, USA'.

The correction is incomplete in a way that misleads. It suggests the gap between 87% and 63% comes from a different census year ('Re-running the analysis on 2000 census data'; 'depends on the census year'). But Golle also re-ran the 1990 data himself and got 61%: 'We found that in 1990 (resp. 2000), only 61% (resp. 63%) of the US population was uniquely' identifiable. He says he 'can not explain this discrepancy' and speculates it comes partly from how the 1990 census tabulates ZIP codes. So the gap is methodological, not a change over time. The correction is rewritten to say so.

fieldFixes.correction: The 87% figure is Latanya Sweeney's estimate from 1990 census data, counting people who 'likely' had a unique combination. Philippe Golle (2006) broadly agreed with her finding. Re-running the analysis himself, though, he found about 61% on the same 1990 data and 63% on 2000 census data. He could not explain the gap and suspected it lay partly in how the 1990 census tabulated data by ZIP code. The underlying point stands: a few 'anonymous' attributes can single out most people. But the exact percentage depends on the data and the method.

issues: All three quotes --check FOUND. The en banc order is 'Filed September 30, 1999' and withdraws 176 F.3d 1132. The panel opinion reads 'Decided May 6, 1999'.

WRONG DATE: the correction says 'in 2002 the district court dismissed the remaining case on ripeness grounds'. Only the oral argument was in 2002 (18 October 2002). Bernstein's own press release is dated 'Chicago, 15 October 2003' and reports that Chief Judge Marilyn Hall Patel 'dismissed Bernstein's case without deciding the constitutionality of the current regulations'. Wikipedia likewise gives 15 October 2003. The document index at cr.yp.to/export/docs.html lists '2002.10.18: B to public' and '2003.10.15: B to public'. Corrected to October 2003.

The panel holding is paraphrased as 'a prior restraint on scientific expression'. The opinion actually holds the rules 'constitute a prior restraint on speech that offends the First Amendment', and says they 'burden[] scientific expression'. Reworded.

Missing context that could mislead readers into thinking no appellate court has bound itself on the question: the Sixth Circuit in Junger v. Daley, 209 F.3d 481 (4 April 2000), held that 'computer source code ... is protected by the First Amendment', which is binding in that circuit. Added with its source.
Source 1 (cr.yp.to status page) is dated '2002', but the page describes the 2003 dismissal. It is undated, so the date is changed to the access year.

fieldFixes.correction: The district court held that source code was speech (April 1996) and struck down the export rules (December 1996 for the ITAR, August 1997 for the EAR). A Ninth Circuit panel affirmed on 6 May 1999, holding that the rules were a prior restraint on speech. But on 30 September 1999 the Ninth Circuit withdrew that panel opinion for rehearing en banc. Before the rehearing, the government loosened the regulations in January 2000 and the case went back to the district court. In October 2003 that court dismissed it without ruling on the new rules, telling Bernstein he could return if there was 'a concrete threat of enforcement'. The 1999 panel opinion is widely cited, but it was withdrawn and is not binding precedent. A binding appellate holding that source code is protected by the First Amendment came instead from the Sixth Circuit in Junger v. Daley (4 April 2000).
